Title: Interactive smart home technologies for users with visual disabilities: a systematic mapping of the literature
Authors: Otavio De Faria Oliveira; Andre Pimenta Freire; Raphael Winckler De Bettio
Journal/conference: International Journal of Computer Applications in Technology, 67(4), 324-? (end page not verified)
Research area: Smart home / ambient assisted living for blind and VI users
Problem addressed: Fragmented knowledge on how interactive smart-home technology serves users with visual disabilities.
Target population: Published studies of smart-home technologies for VI users.
Methodology: Systematic mapping study: 265 papers retrieved, 25 selected.
Technology: Voice, gesture, touch, keyboard and ambient sensors on desktop, mobile, embedded and stand-alone devices.
Main findings: Multimodal interaction and accessible mobile/desktop control interfaces dominate; authors give design implications for VI smart homes.
Limitations: Mapping study (breadth not depth); only 25 primary studies; details of quality appraisal not verified.
Research gaps: Explicitly flags as open: how to overcome barriers from legacy inaccessible utilities, and how to improve user-research methods in this area.
Relevance to SPARSH: Directly motivates SPARSH: most Indian homes have legacy (non-smart) modular switchboards; SPARSH retrofits them rather than replacing them with smart switches.
Design implications: Frame SPARSH as a low-cost retrofit for legacy utilities; keep a non-digital daily-use path (caps) since smart-home approaches need connectivity and new hardware.

Title: Assistive technology use in domestic activities by people who are blind
Authors: Lily M. Turkstra; Tanya Bhatia; Alexa Van Os; Michael Beyeler
Problem addressed: How blind people combine low- and high-tech AT for instrumental activities of daily living.
Target population: 16 legally/completely blind adults aged 25-79, Santa Barbara, USA; most lived with a sighted spouse.
Methodology: Semi-structured interviews (45-90 min) across 7 domestic tasks; thematic content analysis, two coders.
Technology: Bump dots, braille labels, Be My Eyes/Aira, Seeing AI, OrCam, voice assistants.
Main findings: All participants used tactile labels (bump dots, textured stickers, braille) incl. on appliance controls and laundry buttons; touchscreen appliances a major barrier; people try their own senses and tactile aids first and digital tools last; barriers to high-tech: learning curve, inaccuracy, updates, cost, privacy.
Limitations: Small US sample recruited via blindness organisations; self-report; English only; does not discuss wall switches.
Research gaps: Wall switches specifically not studied; non-Western contexts absent.
Relevance to SPARSH: Strong evidence that tactile labelling is a universal, preferred everyday strategy - supports SPARSH's offline tactile-cap daily-use path and sighted-companion setup.
Design implications: Daily use must not depend on a phone; caps must be durable and removable; tactile-first, digital-as-backup.

Title: Collaborative Accessibility: How Blind and Sighted Companions Co-Create Accessible Home Spaces
Authors: Stacy M. Branham; Shaun K. Kane
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 33rd Annual ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '15), pp. 2373-2382
Problem addressed: How blind and sighted household members jointly make homes accessible.
Target population: 10 pairs of close companions (one blind, one sighted).
Main findings: Companions actively co-create accessibility ('collaborative accessibility'); differing abilities sometimes make divergent needs hard to manage.
Research gaps: Calls for technologies supporting collaboration at home.
Relevance to SPARSH: Theoretical grounding for SPARSH's caregiver-sets-up / blind-user-uses model.
Design implications: Design the caregiver flow as collaboration: blind user chooses which switches to label and tests caps; avoid caregiver-only decisions.

Title: "Accessibility Came by Accident": Use of Voice-Controlled Intelligent Personal Assistants by People with Disabilities
Authors: Alisha Pradhan; Kanika Mehta; Leah Findlater
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 2018 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '18), pp. 1-13
Problem addressed: How people with disabilities use smart speakers.
Target population: 346 Amazon Echo reviews by users with disabilities; 16 interviewed users (focus on VI).
Main findings: Widely used despite barriers; VI users need richer voice apps and better discoverability.
Relevance to SPARSH: Shows the smart-home alternative (voice control) requires new devices and connectivity - contrast with SPARSH's zero-electronics daily path.
Design implications: Position SPARSH as complementary to (not competing with) voice control for low-resource homes.
